control_ladder.note_beginner: Once the bulbs are up, do not leave the bed as it stands. Pull any onion plants still in the ground, including the stray ones that sprouted on their own, and rake up the loose tops and skins. Thrips ride out the winter in onion material lying on the soil, so a bed cleaned at the end of the season gives them less to start from next spring.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Thrips tabaci overwinters in onion material left on the soil surface, and volunteer onions carry it through as well, so the end-of-season cleanup is where the carryover is cut. Take out every onion still standing, volunteers included, and get the debris off the bed rather than leaving it on the surface where the insects sit. It is a fall task with a spring payoff: the population that builds through the first warm, dry spell starts from whatever was left behind.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Feed the onions enough and no more. Nitrogen is the part of fertilizer that pushes leafy growth, and piling it on makes thrips worse rather than better. Do not try to outgrow the pest with extra feeding either: a strong, well-watered plant puts up with the feeding better, but it does not end up with fewer thrips on it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Hold nitrogen at adequate rather than heavy, since excess promotes Thrips tabaci. The distinction worth keeping in mind is that vigor buys tolerance of the feeding rather than fewer thrips, so the aim is a plant strong enough to size its bulb through the rasping, not a heavier feeding program. Restraint here is a preventive habit, settled when the feeding is planned rather than once the silvering shows.

control_ladder.note_beginner: While the numbers are still light, a hard jet of water from the hose knocks thrips off. Aim into the crease where the leaves meet, since that is where they shelter. Spray early in the day so the leaves dry off, and keep the plants healthy and watered so they can carry the feeding they do get. If an infestation keeps building past this, your local extension office can tell you what is recommended in your area.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful water knock-down is the response to a light infestation, worked into the leaf axils where the insects sit. Those same folds are why coverage-dependent materials tend to underperform here, so vigor and steady water matter alongside the physical pass. Keep the pass to early in the day so foliage is not left wet, and take a persistent outbreak to local extension guidance rather than to a material named here.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Not every small insect on the onions is a problem. Minute pirate bugs and lacewings both hunt thrips, and they will do some of the work for you as long as you let them. That means holding off on any spray that kills insects in general, since it takes out the helpers along with the thrips and leaves nothing in the bed to check the next wave.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Minute pirate bugs and lacewings help hold Thrips tabaci down, and they do it only where broad-spectrum sprays are avoided, so the conservation choice comes first: a general insecticide removes the predators along with the pest and leaves the thrips to rebuild in the leaf axils where the spray missed them anyway. Lean on the predators through a light infestation, and treat a persistent outbreak per local extension guidance rather than reaching for a broad material.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Put this year's onions on ground that grew no onions or onion relatives last year. The fly spends the winter as a pupa, its resting stage, in the soil around last year's onions, and it comes up in spring right where those plants stood. Choose the new bed well away from that spot, and away from any heap of discarded onions, since the fly keeps going on those between crops.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Delia antiqua pupates in the soil around last season's onions, so a bed that carried alliums is the emergence site for the spring flight and the new planting belongs off it. Distance matters as well as sequence: site the crop away from last year's allium ground and from any cull pile, because culls and volunteer onions carry the fly between crops. Rotation is the decision the cover and the cleanup both rest on, and it is settled before anything is planted.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If your growing season is long enough, wait to plant until the first wave of flies has come and gone. The flies show up with the cool, wet weather of mid-spring and lay their eggs at the base of young plants, so onions that go in after that wave take less damage. Ask your local extension office when the flight usually runs where you live, since the timing shifts from place to place, and do not delay so long that the onions run out of season.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Where the season allows it, delaying planting until the first flight has passed reduces damage, since the first Delia antiqua flight arrives with the cool, wet weather of mid-spring and lays at the base of seedlings and sets. The trade is against the season the crop has left, so this move in time suits a long season and costs a short one. Emergence dates shift with region and year, so confirm the local flight period rather than carrying a calendar date across regions.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Get rid of the onions you rejected at harvest, the undersized or damaged ones, and pull any onion plants that come up on their own, because the fly breeds on both between crops. Take that material out of the garden rather than leaving it in a heap by the bed. In spring, keep fresh manure and freshly turned-in green cover crops out of the onion bed too: the fly is drawn to lay its eggs where something is rotting in the soil.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Two reservoirs and one attractant. Culls and volunteer onions carry Delia antiqua between crops, so remove both and take them out of the garden rather than starting a cull pile, which is exactly what keeps the fly going. Rotting organic matter draws egg-laying, so spring manure and green manure stay out of the bed in the weeks when the first flight is looking for a place to lay.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cover the seedlings or sets with row-cover fabric on planting day, before the spring flight begins, and weight or bury the edges so nothing crawls under. The fly lays its eggs at the base of the plant, so a sealed cover keeps the eggs off the crop. Do not put the cover over ground that grew onions or their relatives last year: the flies come up out of that soil, and a cover over it seals them in with the crop. Use it only on rotated ground.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Exclusion works here only under two conditions. Timing: the cover goes on from planting, ahead of the spring flight, sealed at the edges, because Delia antiqua lays at the base of the plant and a late or loose cover is no barrier. Siting: the pupae overwinter in the soil around last season's onions, so a bed that carried alliums last year seals the emerging flies in with the crop if it is covered. Reserve the fabric for rotated ground.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on the fertilizer, especially nitrogen, the part that drives leafy top growth. Too much of it is one of two things that make neck rot worse, and both are in your hands: the other is bending green tops over to hurry the bulbs along. Feed the onions moderately through the season and let the bulbs mature on their own schedule rather than pushing them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Two aggravating factors sit behind neck rot, excess nitrogen and green tops bent over, and both are grower choices rather than weather. Excess nitrogen worsens a rot that takes immature or insufficiently cured necks, so restraint in the feeding program is the first of the two to settle, and it is settled through the season because there is nothing to correct at lifting. The second is settled at harvest by letting the tops mature on their own.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Leave the tops alone until they fall over by themselves, then lift the onions and dry them thoroughly before they go into storage. Curing, the drying-down of the neck and outer skins, is what keeps this mold out, because it takes hold in necks that were still green or were not dried enough. Store the cured bulbs cool and dry, set aside any that are soft, bruised or spotted to use first, and check white onions soonest, since they are the most prone.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Neck rot starts at the neck in storage, so it is headed off at lifting and in the curing that follows. Let the tops mature naturally rather than knocking them down to force bulbing, since Botrytis enters through immature or insufficiently cured necks and a top bent green leaves exactly that. Cure thoroughly, then store cool and dry, since an insufficiently cured neck is the other opening Botrytis takes. White-skinned bulbs are the most susceptible, so they are the first to check in storage.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start at the seed rack. If a variety is sold as resistant to basal rot, choose it, because this fungus lives in the soil for years and a plant that resists it is the cheapest protection you can buy. Resistance is not offered in every variety, so if you cannot find it, go ahead with rotation and gentle handling rather than waiting on it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Where a resistant variety is available, choose it; the decision is made at seed-buying time, before anything is in the ground, and it costs nothing in the bed. Availability, not value, is the qualifier: resistance is not offered in every variety, so take it where a catalog offers it and keep the rotation and the gentle handling in place whether or not one does.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep onions and their relatives out of a bed that has had this rot for several years, not just one. The fungus lives in the soil itself, so it is still there long after the sick bulbs are gone, and it likes warm ground. Plan several seasons away before onions or any relative go back in, because a single year off does little against something that lasts that long.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotate out of alliums for several years. The pathogen is soilborne, persists for years, and is favored by warm soil, so the length of the break is the substance of the step: a single year away leaves the population where it was. Keep the maggot program running alongside it, since maggot damage is one of the two openings this fungus uses to get into a bulb.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Handle the bulbs gently from lifting through storage: no dropping, no tossing, no nicking them with a fork or knife. This fungus gets into a bulb through a wound, or through the damage maggots leave, and it rots the bulb from the bottom in the field and in storage. Any bulb that is cut or bruised goes to the kitchen first rather than into the storage crate, since one rotting bulb spreads to the ones it touches.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Gentle handling closes an entry route rather than acting on the fungus: wounds and maggot feeding are what open a bulb to Fusarium, and the rot then runs upward from the basal plate in the field and in storage alike. Lift and cure without bruising or cutting, and keep any damaged bulb out of storage to use first, because a rotting bulb passes the problem to what it touches. This guards bulbs that were sound at lifting and cannot rescue one the fungus reached in the bed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Of everything you can do about pink root, a resistant variety does the most. Look for a variety sold as resistant to pink root, and ask your seed supplier which ones hold up in your area, because the fungus comes in different strains and a variety that resists one may not resist another. A resistant variety is chosen once, when you buy seed, and from then on the plant does the defending itself.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resistant varieties are the best control for pink root on onion, ahead of rotation, and the choice is local: resistance varies with the strain of Setophoma terrestris, so ask the seed supplier which varieties hold up in your area rather than relying on a catalog description alone. The fungus penetrates roots directly, without a wound, and builds with every onion crop on the same ground.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give onions a bed that has had no onions or any of their relatives in it for three to six years. The fungus builds up a little more with every onion crop grown on the same ground, and it hangs on in the soil for years, so rotation lowers the amount of it in the bed but does not get rid of it. Treat the break as a way to keep the disease down, and lean on a resistant variety to do the rest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotate off allium ground for three to six years, and hold the expectation in check: rotation reduces pink root rather than clearing it, because Setophoma terrestris persists in soil for years and builds with every onion crop on the same ground. The disease is most common where alliums are grown repeatedly and in warm soils, with the fungus most active at soil temperatures of 75 to 85°F, so a long break lowers the inoculum the next crop meets without resetting it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the onion bed is heavy clay or stays wet after rain, fix the drainage before you plant. This fungus does worse damage in heavy, poorly drained soil, and it hits weak, stressed plants hardest, so a bed that drains well takes away one of the conditions it does best in. A raised bed is the usual fix on heavy ground, and it is standard practice there rather than something to wait on until the roots turn pink.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Heavy, poorly drained soil makes pink root worse, and weak or stressed plants are the most susceptible; drainage settles the first of those directly. Improve drainage on heavy ground before planting, with a raised bed as the standard fix on vegetables, and treat it as a site decision; the pink-to-red shriveling of the roots is the outcome it is meant to prevent, not the signal to start.
